newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong works out post-colonial election plan.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong works out post-colonial election plan.

text.p: Hong Kong's new government on Tuesday set about fine-tuning a post-colonial election plan that has aroused protests from pro-democracy groups who were ousted when Britain handed the territory back to China six weeks ago.

The inner cabinet, or Executive Council (Exco), of China- backed leader Tung Chee-hwa met to work out the broad guidelines for polls to be held by next May, one of the most crucial issues facing the post-handover government, an official said.
"Urgent issues facing the administration will be discussed. I believe electoral arrangements is one," he said.
Tuesday's Exco meeting was the fourth since the body was inaugurated after the July 1 sovereignty.
The 1998 polls will elect a 60-member Legislative Council to replace the China-appointed Provisional Legislature.
China installed the present chamber on July 1, ousting an elected body whose four-year term had two more years to run.

The interim body was swamped with criticism even before it took office. Certain laws which it enacted, especially one to deport young China migrants, and another freezing labour rights, will be challenged in court in the weeks ahead.
These emotive issues threaten to throw into question the legality of the body itself.

The Hong Kong government's Constitutional Affairs Bureau also presented electoral plans to a committee of the interim chamber on Tuesday including a proposal to set up an Electoral Affairs Commission to monitor the 1998 elections.

Bureau officials told a panel of legislators the commission will draw boundaries for five geographical constituencies where 20 legislative seats will be directly elected. It would also monitor the polls and handle the registration of voters.
Under the plan Hong Kong will scrap a first-past-the-post election method in geographical constituencies in favour of proportional representation.
Functional constituencies based on economic sectors and professions will fill 30 seats by indirect elections.
The other 10 seats will be filled in an indirect election by an 800-member committee drawn from the functional constituencies as well as from other elites and grassroots groups.
Critics have said that under the new rules pro-democracy parties are unlikely to repeat their strong 1995 showing in which they won the largest bloc of seats in the ousted assembly.
The run-up to next year's polls will be closely watched.

Eralier this month August accused Britain of meddling in its internal affairs after London announced it would keep a close eye on in Hong Kong and urged "free and fair elections" to be held as soon as possible.
Sino-British ties sank to one of their lowest points when former governor Chris Patten launched electoral reforms in the last years of colonial rule despite fierce opposition by China.
